questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Plus-que-parfait against passe compose
questions.learningObjective: separate an earlier completed action from the past event that anchors it
questions.stem: A narrator sets two events in order: « J'avais fini le travail avant midi ; le directeur est arrivé à treize heures. » What does the plus-que-parfait mark that the passe compose does not?

options.text: an action already complete before the other past action began
an action that lasted the whole morning without ever finishing
options.misconception: reads the plus-que-parfait as the imperfect and hears duration in it

options.text: an action the speaker only heard about from somebody else
options.misconception: confuses tense of priority with reported information from another source

options.text: an action the speaker repeats every single working day
options.misconception: takes a single completed action for a repeated habit

questions.explanation: Le plus-que-parfait states that one action was finished before another past action started, so the finished work stands strictly earlier than the arrival that anchors the narrative. The passe compose in « le directeur est arrivé » is that anchor: it is the reference point, not the earlier action. The trap is « avant midi », which is an adverb of time and not a tense. A learner who lets the adverb carry the priority writes « j'ai fini le travail avant midi », which reports two events that merely happen in that order and gives up the claim that the first was complete before the second began.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two actions the other one is being measured against.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Imparfait against passe compose
questions.learningObjective: name the aspect that separates background situation from interrupting event
questions.stem: Two lines from one account sit side by side: « Il pleuvait depuis une heure » and « Soudain, l'orage a éclaté. » Which contrast does the pair of tenses draw?

options.text: a situation running on, and the event that interrupted it
one event reported twice by two separate witnesses
options.misconception: reads the two tenses as two tellers of the same happening

options.text: a morning habit the speaker has since given up
options.misconception: treats the imperfect as a habit and ignores the change of state

options.text: a morning forecast about what the afternoon held
options.misconception: confuses the imperfect of weather with the imperfect of prediction

questions.explanation: L'imparfait describes a situation the speaker looks at from inside, without pointing at its start or its end, and « il pleuvait depuis une heure » is exactly that: rain with no beginning and no finish in view. Le passé composé frames an action from outside as one finished, bounded occasion, which is what « l'orage a éclaté » is, and « soudain » names the moment the first situation stops. The trap is the reverse move, using the passé composé for the long background because the background happens to be made of a verb of duration; « il a plu depuis une heure » points at a single completed spell of rain rather than at rain that was still going on.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two clauses could have a start time marked on it.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Subjonctif with expressions of doubt
questions.learningObjective: justify the subjonctif after a negated verb of belief
questions.stem: A student says: « Je ne crois pas qu'il vienne demain au marché. » What exactly is the subjonctif marking in this sentence?

options.text: the doubt that « ne ... pas croire » carries about the future
the politeness that the negation adds to an otherwise flat claim
options.misconception: reads negation as a courtesy rather than as a reversal of belief

options.text: the certainty the speaker holds about tomorrow's arrangements
options.misconception: treats any verb after « croire » as needing the subjonctif

options.text: the doubt that the pronoun « il » carries by itself
options.misconception: believes a third person pronoun can select a mood

questions.explanation: Doubt, negation, emotion, necessity and concession all ask the speaker to leave the fact unclaimed, and French marks that with the subjonctif. Here « je ne crois pas » denies the belief, so what follows is reported as unsettled and « qu'il vienne » keeps the subjonctif. The same verb without the negation takes the indicative, since « je crois qu'il vient » presents a fact the speaker holds to be true. That asymmetry is the trap: « croire » is a verb of belief, so learners half remember the indicative and half remember the subjonctif, and the negation is the only thing that decides between them.
questions.hint: Remove the negation and see which mood the verb of belief would take.

questions.topic: Subjonctif with expressions of emotion
questions.learningObjective: choose the mood that follows a state of feeling about an earlier event
questions.stem: A colleague writes: « Je suis désolée que tu aies raté le train. » Which group of expressions puts the subjonctif in that clause?

options.text: expressions of feeling such as regret, joy and disappointment
expressions of proof such as evidence, marks and witnesses
options.misconception: takes any noun after « que » to be a reportable fact

options.text: expressions of timing such as dates, hours and seasons
options.misconception: believes a time expression pulls the mood down to the subjonctif

options.text: expressions of measure such as weight, height and length
options.misconception: confuses a quantifier phrase with an emotional reaction

questions.explanation: « Être désolé, heureux, fâché, surpris » followed by « que » states a reaction, and a reaction does not claim that its cause is a settled fact, so the subjonctif follows. The cause sits earlier than the feeling, which is why the verb inside the clause is a plus-que-parfait: « que tu aies raté » puts the missed train before the regret about it. The trap is that « je suis désolée » is a statement of the speaker's own state, and a learner who hears a statement of fact reaches for the indicative, writing « je suis désolée que tu as raté », which reports the reaction as though the cause were the plain content of the news.

questions.topic: Subjonctif with expressions of necessity
questions.learningObjective: pick the mood that an impersonal necessity demands
questions.stem: A workshop notice reads: « Il faut que chaque pièce soit vérifiée avant l'assemblage. » What is forcing « soit vérifiée » into the subjonctif?

the passive voice that this particular clause is written in
options.misconception: believes the passive itself selects the subjonctif

options.text: the forward reference to time found in the phrase before
options.misconception: thinks a mention of future time drives the mood choice

options.text: the fact that the subject of the clause is a machine part
options.misconception: lets the kind of subject decide the mood of the clause

questions.explanation: « Il faut que » states a requirement without naming who imposes it, and a requirement leaves the action open rather than reported as done, so the subjonctif comes after it. Learners tend to keep the que from the first pattern and pair it with an infinitive, producing « il faut que vérifier », which is not a shape French builds; the two patterns are alternatives, and the presence or absence of a subject decides which one is used.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Subjonctif with expressions of concession
questions.learningObjective: recognise the concessive conjunction that demands the subjonctif
questions.stem: A guest apologises for arriving late: « Bien que je sois en retard, je viendrai quand même. » Which word of the first clause carries the concessive sense?

options.text: « Bien que », which opens a clause against the speaker's own interest
« en retard », which gives the reason for the lateness
options.misconception: reads an excuse phrase as the cause of what follows

options.text: « je », which marks the person who concedes the point
options.misconception: thinks a pronoun can signal a logical relation

options.text: « viendrai », which names the event that is being granted
options.misconception: puts the concession inside the main clause instead of the subordinated one

questions.explanation: « Bien que » concedes a fact that works against the speaker while the main clause asserts something that goes on regardless, and that opposition is what puts the subjonctif into « je sois ». The everyday alternative is « mais », which takes the indicative, so « je suis en retard, mais je viendrai » is not wrong. The trap is that « bien que » behaves in speech like « mais » and a learner supplies the mood that goes with « mais », writing « bien que je suis en retard ». questions.topic: Conditionnel present for a hypothesis
questions.learningObjective: identify which clause of a conditional pair holds the hypothesis
questions.stem: A colleague proposes: « Si nous réservions la salle demain, nous aurions le temps de répétér. » Which verb form is holding the hypothesis open?

options.text: the present conditional on « si nous réservions »
the imperfect on « nous aurions », the real condition of the pair
options.misconception: misreads a conditional as an imperfect and loses the consequence

options.text: the present tense on « si », which announces a settled fact
options.misconception: takes every si-clause to state something known to be true

options.text: the future tense hidden inside « nous répétons » that is implied
options.misconception: supposes a future is present because the talk is about tomorrow

questions.explanation: In the conditional pair the opening clause states what is being supposed and the main clause states what would follow, and here « si nous réservions » is the supposition while « nous aurions le temps » is the consequence of it. A hypothesis about the future is carried by the present conditional, and in ordinary speech the imperfect after « si » does the same work, as in « si nous réservions » standing in for « si nous réserverions ». The trap is the future in the si-clause: « si nous réserverons » is not a hypothesis at all but a prediction, so the sentence claims the booking will happen rather than supposing it.

questions.topic: Conditionnel passe for a regret
questions.learningObjective: explain why a hypothetical past conclusion avoids the passe compose
questions.stem: An old photograph prompts: « Si j'avais su pour la montagne, je n'y serais pas allé. » What is the past conditional doing in the second clause?

options.text: carrying the consequence of a past condition the speaker now denies
reporting a fact the speaker is certain actually took place
options.misconception: hears the conditional as a firm claim about the past

options.text: announcing a plan the speaker made and then dropped on purpose
options.misconception: takes the conditional as a statement of intention

options.text: quoting an order the speaker was given and then refused
options.misconception: reads the pair as reported speech with its own mood

questions.explanation: « Si j'avais su » sets a condition the speaker now holds to be false, and « je n'y serais pas allé » gives the consequence that would have followed had it been true. A learner translating word for word produces exactly that, and the result no longer registers as a regret but as a plain report of something that happened.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Conditionnel de politesse
questions.learningObjective: explain what the polite conditional does to a request in French
questions.stem: A neighbour writes: « Pourriez-vous, s'il vous plaît, baisser le volume après vingt-deux heures ? » What work is the conditional doing for the writer?

options.text: framing the request as a favour instead of an instruction
reporting that the volume is already low enough for her
options.misconception: reads the conditional as a claim about the present state

options.text: recalling that the volume was high on one earlier evening
options.misconception: mistakes a softened request for a report of the past

options.text: making the hour something the neighbour must agree to in writing
options.misconception: believes politeness here turns the sentence into a contract

questions.explanation: French has a conditional set aside for softening an ask: « pourriez-vous », « auriez-vous l'obligeance », « accepteriez-vous ». The plain form is not a neutral version of it, because the vous form of the present is itself formal, so « Vous baissez le volume » sounds like an order. What the conditional adds is the distance that lets the speaker ask rather than tell, and it asks for a hypothetical ability that the addressee may decline. The trap is reading the mood as information, so the sentence becomes a statement that the neighbour is already able to lower the volume, which is not what the writer intended to assert.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Relative pronouns qui and que
questions.learningObjective: assign each of the two pronouns to the role it plays in its clause
questions.stem: A sentence offers two relatives: « Le livre que j'ai acheté » and « L'auteur qui a écrit ce livre. » What does each pronoun stand for?

options.text: que points at a thing, and qui points at a person
que points at a person, and qui points at a thing
options.misconception: swaps the two pronouns because the words sound alike

options.text: que points at the action, and qui points at the speaker
options.misconception: treats a relative pronoun as a name for the verb

options.text: que points at a whole clause, and qui points at its subject
options.misconception: assumes que is always used for clauses rather than things

questions.explanation: « Que » is the accusative form and stands for the direct object of the verb in the relative clause, which is why it refers to a thing: « le livre que j'ai acheté » is the thing bought. « Qui » is the subject form and refers to the doer, here a person: « l'auteur qui a écrit » is the one who wrote. A thing can also take « qui » when it is the subject, as in « le livre qui m'a plu », so the division is by grammatical role and not by kind of noun. The trap is the one the preposition creates: after « à », « de » or « pour » only « qui », « quoi », « dont » and « où » are available, and « que » is not one of them.
questions.hint: Ask whether the pronoun is the one doing the verb in the small clause.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Relative pronouns ou, dont and auquel
questions.learningObjective: match place, possession and preposition to the right relative form
questions.stem: Three relatives appear in one report: « la ville où je suis né », « l'homme dont le fils est malade », « le dossier auquel je travaille. » Which form does each job need?

options.text: « où » for place, « dont » for possession, « auquel » after « à »
« où » for possession, « dont » for place, « auquel » for time
options.misconception: assigns each of the three forms to the wrong relationship

options.text: « dont » for place, « auquel » for possession, « où » after « à »
options.misconception: swaps possession with place and moves the preposition case

options.text: « auquel » for place, « où » for possession, « dont » after « à »
options.misconception: believes « auquel » is the general form for every relation

questions.explanation: Place is « où », which stands for « dans » or « à » plus the place, and it can also stand for a moment, as in « le jour où il est parti ». Possession is « dont », which comes from « de » and stands for the possessor, so « l'homme dont le fils est malade » is the man whose son is ill. A preposition keeps its own case, so « à » plus the noun gives « auquel », with « le quel », « du quel » and « au quel » as the other forms. The trap is reaching for « que » after a preposition, since « que » cannot be governed by anything in French, and « le dossier que je travaille » is not a sentence a speaker accepts.
questions.hint: Ask which preposition the relationship is built on in each case.

questions.learningObjective: recognise when the antecedent is a whole clause rather than a noun
questions.stem: A report ends: « Il a plu toute la journée, ce qui a gâché notre promenade. » What stands in front of « ce qui »?

the word « journée », which stands for the length of the time
options.misconception: grabs the nearest noun and treats it as the antecedent

options.text: the noun « promenade », which the pronoun is said to replace
options.misconception: sits the pronoun at the end and reads it backwards over the clause

options.text: the writer, who is the subject the sentence leaves implied
options.misconception: takes a missing subject as the thing being referred to

The trap is hunting for the nearest noun, because « journée » is much closer than the subject and seems like the natural thing to point at, and « ce que » behaves the same way, taking a whole clause where « ce qui » is also possible with no antecedent at all.

questions.topic: Indefinite article and the partitive that follows
questions.learningObjective: apply the partitive that an indefinite article forces on the noun
questions.stem: A shopping list reads: « du pain, de la farine, de l'eau minérale, des pommes. » Why does every noun on it take a partitive?

options.text: an indefini in front of it has to be followed by a partitive
all four nouns are uncountable, so they need no article at all
options.misconception: believes the partitive exists to rescue uncountable nouns

options.text: the list names goods the shopper has already bought earlier
options.misconception: reads the partitive as ownership already in hand

options.text: the whole list happens to be written in the plural form
options.misconception: attributes the article to the grammatical number of the line

questions.explanation: « Du », « de la », « de l' » and « des » are the indefinites, and a noun that follows one of them takes a partitive rather than « un » or « une »: « du pain », « de la farine », « de l'eau », « du riz », « des pommes ». The two narrow exceptions are « un de », as in « un de mes amis », and a handful of fixed expressions, so the rule holds almost everywhere; the trap is reaching back for « un » and writing « un pain » where the pattern has already committed to a partitive.

questions.topic: Negation with a pronoun and its word order
questions.learningObjective: place a pronoun correctly inside a negated clause
questions.stem: A colleague says: « Je n'ai rien mangé ce matin. » Why does « rien » sit in front of the verb in that sentence?

options.text: a pronoun stands where the object would stand in the affirmative
« ne » needs a second pronoun in order to close the negation
options.misconception: believes the two halves of a negation are symmetrical in French

options.text: the participle always comes last in a sentence built with ne
options.misconception: takes the negative particle to be a marker of compound tenses

options.text: « rien » is a noun here, so nouns stand before the verb
options.misconception: treats a pronoun of quantity as an ordinary noun in this slot

questions.stem: A host says: « Personne n'est venu et je n'ai rien préparé. » What is each half of that sentence doing?

the first rules out every thing, the second rules out every person

questions.topic: Ne jamais and ne plus distinguished
questions.learningObjective: tell the two lookalike negations apart by their timeline
questions.stem: A former member says: « Je ne joue plus du tout et je ne joue jamais le dimanche. » How do the two negations differ?

« plus » rules out one day; « jamais » ends the habit for good
options.misconception: reads « plus » as a particular day and « jamais » as the end

the action becomes something she only said rather than did

answer.exemplar: Step one asks whether the speaker could point at the moment. « J'ai mangé une pomme » passes, because a single apple at a single sitting can be dated. Step two asks what the other half of the clause is doing, and that is where the imperfect earns its place. On « Nous passions au marché quand il a plu », the rain is a bounded event, so « a plu » is the compound past, and the walking is read from inside the rain rather than dated. On « Nous étions au marché quand il a plu », the same contrast appears with « étions » as a state, which is the commonest imperfect in a real sentence. questions.topic: Teaching the three uses of the conditional
questions.learningObjective: separate hypothesis, regret and politeness in the same mood
questions.stem: A learner asks how many jobs the conditional does in French. Explain the three uses and show each one working in a sentence you write yourself.

answer.exemplar: Three, and each is easier to place once it is tied to a moment in time. The hypothesis lives in the present: si j'avais le temps, je partirais, where the si-clause supposes and the main clause gives what would follow. The regret lives in the past: si j'avais su, je ne serais pas venu, where the past conditional carries a consequence of something that never happened. The polite request lives outside time altogether: pourriez-vous m'aider un instant, which asks rather than instructs. Add the reported future and the family is complete, since elle a dit qu'elle viendrait is the future one step further from the speaker. The error to warn about is the conditional used as a plain future, so « je pensais qu'il viendrait » reports a belief held then, while « je pensais qu'il viendra » states a belief held now.

questions.explanation: The conditional is usually taught as one mood with several jobs, which leaves learners unable to say why a sentence feels odd. The tidier account ties each job to a time: the present conditional supposes and asks, the past conditional regrets what did not happen, and reported speech borrows the present conditional to stand one step behind the future. Once the times are sorted, a mistake becomes visible as a mismatch, such as a past conditional opening a supposition about the present or a present conditional carrying the consequence of a past regret. The politeness use is the one that sits outside the tense system, and it is best taught as a separate habit attached to a request.

Future becomes present conditional, so « je viendrai » is reported as « il a dit qu'il viendrait ». Two things stay put. A verb of saying in the past keeps its own tense, and so does a fact that is still true and very recent, which is why « il dit qu'il est fatigué » is heard in speech and is not a mistake. What changes beyond the tense is the question, and that is worth teaching with the table rather than beside it, since a reported question gives up its inversion and lets « si » or a question word take the place.

The reason is that a report necessarily stands at a different point in time from the thing reported, so each tense is pushed one step away from the speaker. Two exceptions keep the lesson honest: a still-true and very recent fact may stay in the present, and quoted speech word for word keeps everything as written. Adding the question to the same lesson is efficient, because both changes come from the same cause, namely that the report no longer stands face to face with the event.

questions.topic: Order of moves when turning an order into a report
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps that convert a spoken order into a report
questions.stem: Four moves are needed to turn a spoken order into a written report. Which sequence is the only one that produces a finished French sentence?

options.text: Replace the imperative with « que » plus the subjonctif.
Decide who the order is addressed to before choosing a form.
Put the verb of saying into the past to open the report.
Choose between « que » and « de » plus an infinitive.

questions.explanation: A report has to be framed before anything can be reported into it, so the verb of saying goes into the past first and the reader can see from then on that these are somebody's words. The next question is who is being ordered, because that decides whether a third person pronoun has to carry the order. Then the form is chosen: « de » plus an infinitive is the plainer option, and « que » plus the subjonctif is the one to use when the reporter is not the person obeyed, which is the case the fourth step handles. Any sequence that leaves the verb of saying in the present gives a report that is still happening.
questions.hint: Ask which step nothing else can be done before.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Building a paragraph with one controlling idea
questions.learningObjective: order a paragraph so each sentence has a job to do
questions.stem: Four sentences of one short paragraph have been printed out of order. Which sequence gives a paragraph that states a habit, explains it, gives a case and then qualifies it?

options.text: Il reste aujourd'hui quelques classes qui la pratiquent encore.
Autrefois, la lecture à voix haute était partout en usage.
Les horaires ont lourdement changé depuis vingt ans.
Dans mon quartier, on l'a abandonnée dès l'âge de sept ans.

questions.explanation: The paragraph needs a topic before it needs anything else, so the sentence naming the old habit opens it and gives the reader something to hold. The change in schedules then explains why the habit fell, and the sentence about one district turns the general into a case that can be checked. The last sentence qualifies the whole account by admitting what survives, which is what keeps the paragraph from overstating. Run the order the other way and the paragraph opens with an exception nobody can yet place, which is the usual reason a paragraph feels like it has no beginning.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence the other three are all about.

questions.subject: FRENCH
questions.topic: Reporting a question in the second person
questions.learningObjective: apply both changes a direct question needs once it is reported
questions.stem: Stage one: say what changes when « Où est la gare ? » becomes « Il m'a demandé où était la gare. » Stage two: do the same to « Vous venez demain ? »

answer.exemplar: Stage one: two things change and they come from the same cause. The direct question inverts its subject after the verb, and the report drops the inversion so the verb stands next to its subject, and the tense steps back, which turns « est » into the imperfect « était ». The question word stays, because there is no inversion left for it to replace. Stage two: the same two changes on a question with no question word give « Il m'a demandé si je venais demain », because « si » now takes the place of the inversion and the verb has stepped back to the imperfect. Had the second question carried a question word, as in « Où allez-vous demain ? », the report would keep the word and drop the inversion instead, giving « il m'a demandé où j'allais demain ».

questions.explanation: The two changes that a reported question needs are often taught as separate items, and learners end up applying one without the other. They belong together because both come from the same fact: a report is no longer face to face with the event, so the shape of the question and the tense of the verb both move. Setting the two side by side, one with a question word and one without, shows the learner which piece of the direct question each reported form has inherited and which piece it has had to invent.
questions.hint: Ask what the word « si » is standing in for in the report.
